Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Sous chef: The second in command, whose name means under-chef in French; they run the kitchen day to day when the head chef is away.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Pastry chef: Pastry chefs run the dessert and baking side, and the work is so precise, as baking is chemistry, that it is often a separate career path.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Saucier: The saucier makes sauces and stews, one of the most prestigious stations in the brigade, and is often the highest-ranked below sous chef.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Line cook: Line cooks man the stations on the cooking line, where plates are assembled during service at high speed; this is the backbone of the kitchen.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Commis chef: A junior chef in training, whose name is French for assistant, and who learns each station under a chef de partie.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Chef de partie: Also called station chef, this person runs one section, like grill or fish, and the title means chief of a party or section.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Dishwasher: Often the most undervalued job; famously, the writer George Orwell and chef Anthony Bourdain both started out washing dishes.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Garde manger: The cold station for salads, pâtés and charcuterie; the name means keeper of the food, since the role began in preservation.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Head chef: The leader of the kitchen who sets menus and manages staff; the word chef simply means chief in French.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Prep cook: Prep cooks chop, portion and prepare ingredients before service, so the line cooks can cook quickly; it is where many chefs start.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Poissonnier: The fish cook, in the French brigade system created by Auguste Escoffier, who also invented the system of kitchen ranks.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Rôtisseur: The roast cook, who handles roasted and grilled meats; the name comes from the French rôtir, to roast.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Sommelier: A trap: sommeliers are wine experts and work in the dining room, not the kitchen; the word comes from an old French term for a pack-animal driver.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Maître d': Front-of-house head who manages seating and reservations; short for maître d'hôtel, master of the house, and works in the dining room.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Host: The host greets and seats guests at the front of the restaurant, not in the kitchen.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Waiter: Waiters serve at the table and are front of house; kitchen staff rarely meet the customers.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Bartender: Bartenders mix drinks at the bar, not in the kitchen, and the word bartender dates from the 1800s American West.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Busser: Bussers clear and reset tables in the dining room, and the term is from the American word bus for clearing.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Valet: The valet parks cars outside, with a name that comes from French for a manservant.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Cashier: Cashiers handle payments at the front, which is outside the kitchen.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Barback: The barback supports the bartender by restocking ice and bottles, and is not a kitchen role.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Food critic: Critics sit in the dining room judging the food, and a famous one, like a Michelin inspector, can make or break a restaurant.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Barista: Baristas make espresso drinks at the coffee bar, and the word is Italian for bartender, not a kitchen role.
Jobs in a restaurant kitchen.Coat check: The coat check attendant minds jackets at the entrance, a front-of-house job with no cooking involved.

Animals that live in burrows.Mole: A mole's velvety fur lies flat in either direction, so it can move backward in a tunnel, and it can dig about 4 meters an hour.
Animals that live in burrows.Meerkat: Meerkat burrow systems have many entrances, and a sentry stands guard on hind legs, barking at hawks.
Animals that live in burrows.Prairie dog: Their towns can hold thousands, and their calls can describe the size, shape, and color of an approaching predator.
Animals that live in burrows.Rabbit: Wild rabbits live in warrens, networks of burrows, and they can have several litters a year.
Animals that live in burrows.Badger: Badger setts can be centuries old and pass between generations, with dozens of entrances.
Animals that live in burrows.Gopher: A pocket gopher's lips close behind its teeth so it can dig with its mouth without eating dirt.
Animals that live in burrows.Naked mole rat: A naked mole rat lives in a colony ruled by a queen, like bees, and rarely gets cancer, living about 30 years.
Animals that live in burrows.Earthworm: Earthworms tunnel through soil, drawing leaves down and aerating the ground, and Darwin spent years studying them.
Animals that live in burrows.Wombat: A wombat's droppings are cube-shaped, and it digs burrows with powerful claws and a rock-hard rear.
Animals that live in burrows.Groundhog: Groundhogs hibernate in deep burrows, and their heartbeat slows to a few beats a minute.
Animals that live in burrows.Aardvark: Its name means earth pig in Afrikaans, and it digs burrows at night while hunting termites with a sticky tongue.
Animals that live in burrows.Armadillo: A nine-banded armadillo digs dens in the ground and always gives birth to identical quadruplets.
Animals that live in burrows.Fennec fox: Its huge ears radiate heat and listen for prey underground, and it digs burrows in the Sahara.
Animals that live in burrows.Koala: Koalas live high in eucalyptus trees and sleep around 20 hours a day.
Animals that live in burrows.Sloth: Sloths hang from branches, and algae grow in their fur, giving a greenish tint.
Animals that live in burrows.Monkey: Most monkeys live in trees and forage in groups, not in underground burrows.
Animals that live in burrows.Giraffe: The tallest land animal has the same number of neck bones as a human, seven, and sleeps standing, not in a burrow.
Animals that live in burrows.Eagle: Eagles build huge nests called aeries high on cliffs or trees, and some are reused for decades.
Animals that live in burrows.Dolphin: Dolphins sleep with half their brain at a time, and they live in the sea.
Animals that live in burrows.Parrot: Parrots nest in tree holes or cliffs, though a few, like burrowing parrots, do dig into riverbanks.
Animals that live in burrows.Deer: Deer sleep in sheltered spots above ground rather than burrowing, and fawns are hidden in grass.
Animals that live in burrows.Chimpanzee: Chimps make a new sleeping nest from branches in the trees almost every night.
Animals that live in burrows.Flamingo: Flamingos build mud mounds as nests, and their pink color comes from the food they eat.
Animals that live in burrows.Hare: A trap: unlike rabbits, hares don't dig burrows; they rest in shallow ground dents called forms, and their young are born furry and ready to run.

Mexican dishes.Tacos: The Spanish word 'taco' first referred to a plug used in mining, and tacos al pastor were shaped by Lebanese immigrants' shawarma.
Mexican dishes.Enchiladas: The name means 'dressed in chili'; the tortillas are dipped in a chile sauce, then rolled around a filling and baked.
Mexican dishes.Tamales: Maize dough steamed in corn husks or banana leaves; the Aztecs and Maya made them, and families still gather to make them for Christmas.
Mexican dishes.Mole: There are many versions of this complex chile sauce, and Oaxaca is famed for seven moles, some with more than 30 ingredients, including chocolate.
Mexican dishes.Pozole: A hominy stew that the Aztecs are said to have made in ritual feasts; today it is a classic for celebrations.
Mexican dishes.Chilaquiles: A breakfast of fried tortilla pieces simmered in salsa, designed to rescue leftover tortillas and, famously, a hangover.
Mexican dishes.Quesadilla: The name comes from 'queso' for cheese, though in Mexico City it often has no cheese at all unless you ask for it.
Mexican dishes.Tostada: A flat tortilla fried until crisp and used as a plate for toppings, a clever way to use stale tortillas.
Mexican dishes.Elote: Street-food corn on the cob, slathered with mayonnaise, cotija cheese, chili and lime, and sold from carts all over Mexico.
Mexican dishes.Sopes: Thick little corn cakes with a pinched rim that holds beans, meat and salsa; they are sold in markets and street stalls.
Mexican dishes.Cochinita pibil: A Yucatan dish of pork marinated in achiote and sour orange, then slow-cooked wrapped in banana leaves in a pit oven.
Mexican dishes.Birria: A spicy goat or beef stew from Jalisco that became a global craze when served in tacos with a dipping consommé.
Mexican dishes.Arepa: Not Mexican: these corn cakes are a staple in Venezuela and Colombia, often split and stuffed like a sandwich.
Mexican dishes.Pupusa: A stuffed corn tortilla that is the national dish of El Salvador, so it doesn't belong here despite looking similar.
Mexican dishes.Feijoada: Brazil's national dish is a black bean stew with pork, which is sometimes traced back to enslaved people who cooked scraps.
Mexican dishes.Paella: A Spanish rice dish from Valencia, traditionally cooked outdoors over a wood fire in a wide, shallow pan.
Mexican dishes.Gazpacho: A cold tomato soup from Andalusia in Spain, which was made before tomatoes arrived in Europe, with bread and garlic.
Mexican dishes.Chili con carne: Tex-Mex, not Mexican: it was developed in Texas, and in Mexico it is often thought of as an American dish.
Mexican dishes.Chimichurri: A herby Argentine sauce for grilled steak; the green mix of parsley, garlic and vinegar has no Mexican connection.
Mexican dishes.Moussaka: A layered dish of aubergine and minced meat with béchamel, usually considered Greek, though versions appear across the eastern Mediterranean.
Mexican dishes.Pierogi: Polish dumplings filled with potato, cheese or meat, often served with fried onions and sour cream.
Mexican dishes.Pad thai: Thailand's famous stir-fried noodles were popularised in the 1930s and 1940s as a national dish by the country's government.
Mexican dishes.Falafel: These chickpea or fava bean fritters are from the Middle East, and in Egypt they are traditionally made with fava beans.
Mexican dishes.Jambalaya: A rice dish from Louisiana, a Creole cousin of paella; the name may come from Provençal or Spanish words.

Things made from potatoes.French fries: Whether Belgian or French in origin is still debated. Belgians say the fries were first made in the Meuse valley in the 1600s.
Things made from potatoes.Colcannon: Irish dish of mashed potato with cabbage or kale. Charms like a coin or ring were once hidden in it at Halloween.
Things made from potatoes.Latkes: Fried potato pancakes eaten at Hanukkah. Before potatoes reached Europe, they were made from cheese or other ingredients.
Things made from potatoes.Hash browns: Shredded potatoes fried into a crispy cake. The dish came from the nineteenth century and is a diner breakfast staple.
Things made from potatoes.Rösti: The national dish of Swiss Germans, made from grated potato fried until crisp. Its name means crisp and golden.
Things made from potatoes.Pringles: Not simply sliced potato: the crisps are made from a dough of dried potato flakes and wheat starch pressed into saddle shapes.
Things made from potatoes.Tater tots: Invented in 1953 by Ore-Ida founders, who turned leftover potato scraps from fries into small cylinders.
Things made from potatoes.Potato starch: Extracted from crushed potatoes and used to thicken sauces. Its fine powder makes it a favorite for crispy Korean fried chicken.
Things made from potatoes.Lefse: A soft Norwegian flatbread made of potatoes and flour, rolled thin and griddled. It is a Christmas tradition in Scandinavian American homes.
Things made from potatoes.Mashed potatoes: Butter, milk and a ricer make them smooth, while overworking them in a blender releases starch and turns them gluey.
Things made from potatoes.Dauphinoise: French gratin of thinly sliced potatoes baked in cream, from the Dauphiné region. Traditionally it contains no cheese.
Things made from potatoes.Potato chips: According to legend, chef George Crum invented them in 1853 in New York when a customer complained his fries were too thick.
Things made from potatoes.Polenta: Made from cornmeal, not potatoes. Corn is a New World crop, like potatoes, but it grows on a grass.
Things made from potatoes.Tortilla chips: Fried or baked corn masa. They were mass produced in Los Angeles in the 1940s from leftover tortillas.
Things made from potatoes.Hummus: Chickpeas blended with tahini. There are no potatoes, though many cooks add a spoonful for creaminess.
Things made from potatoes.Couscous: Pasta made from semolina wheat, not potatoes. It is steamed, not boiled.
Things made from potatoes.Risotto: Made with rice, not potatoes. Starch released from the rice gives it the creamy texture.
Things made from potatoes.Plantain chips: Slices of plantain, a starchy banana, fried to crisp. They are not potato, though they are a similar snack.
Things made from potatoes.Tapioca: Starch from cassava root, not potato, though both are tubers. They are both from South America.
Things made from potatoes.Sweet potato fries: Sweet potatoes are not true potatoes at all. They belong to the morning glory family, not the nightshades.
Things made from potatoes.Taro chips: Taro is another starchy root, a staple across the Pacific. It is not related to the potato, which is a nightshade.
Things made from potatoes.Grits: Ground corn, not potato. They are a staple of the American South with Native American roots.
Things made from potatoes.Popcorn: Popped corn kernels. Native peoples in the Americas were popping corn thousands of years ago.
Things made from potatoes.Arancini: Fried Sicilian rice balls rather than potato. Their name means little oranges, after their color and shape.

Cities in India.Mumbai: Mumbai is the home of Bollywood, which makes more films each year than Hollywood, and it was once seven separate islands.
Cities in India.Delhi: Delhi has been a capital for centuries, and its old city has the Red Fort and one of India's largest mosques, Jama Masjid.
Cities in India.Bangalore: Bangalore is India's tech hub, nicknamed the Silicon Valley of India, now officially called Bengaluru.
Cities in India.Chennai: Chennai was called Madras until 1996, and its beach, Marina, is among the longest city beaches in the world.
Cities in India.Kolkata: Kolkata was the capital of British India until 1911, and it still has hand-pulled rickshaws and yellow taxis.
Cities in India.Jaipur: Jaipur is the Pink City, painted that color in 1876 to welcome the visiting Prince of Wales.
Cities in India.Agra: Agra is the home of the Taj Mahal, built by Emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
Cities in India.Varanasi: Varanasi is one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, and Hindus bathe in the Ganges from its riverside steps.
Cities in India.Pune: Pune is known as the Oxford of the East, with many universities, and it's a hub of Marathi culture.
Cities in India.Ahmedabad: Ahmedabad was Gandhi's base, and its old walled city became India's first UNESCO World Heritage city in 2017.
Cities in India.Kochi: Kochi, on the Kerala coast, has Chinese fishing nets that hang from cantilevers, and a historic spice trade.
Cities in India.Karachi: Karachi is Pakistan's largest city, a port on the Arabian Sea, and not part of India.
Cities in India.Lahore: Lahore is in Pakistan, close to the Indian border, and is known for its Mughal-era fort and mosque.
Cities in India.Islamabad: Islamabad is Pakistan's capital, a planned city built in the 1960s at the foot of the Margalla Hills.
Cities in India.Dhaka: Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh, and is called the rickshaw capital of the world.
Cities in India.Kathmandu: Kathmandu is Nepal's capital, a valley city with thousands of temples, and the gateway to Everest.
Cities in India.Colombo: Colombo is Sri Lanka's commercial capital, with its official capital at Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte.
Cities in India.Chittagong: Chittagong is Bangladesh's main port, and is famous for its ship-breaking yards.
Cities in India.Peshawar: Peshawar is a city in Pakistan close to the Khyber Pass, among the oldest living cities in South Asia.
Cities in India.Thimphu: Thimphu is Bhutan's capital, and one of the few capitals in the world with no traffic lights.
Cities in India.Malé: Malé is the capital of the Maldives, and one of the world's most densely packed cities on a tiny island.
Cities in India.Kandy: Kandy is a Sri Lankan city, home of the Temple of the Tooth, said to hold a relic of the Buddha.
Cities in India.Kabul: Kabul is Afghanistan's capital, and it lies in a valley around 1,800 meters above sea level.
Cities in India.Rawalpindi: Rawalpindi is in Pakistan, and is the twin city of Islamabad, and the home of the Pakistani army.

Places in Tanzania.Kilimanjaro: Africa's tallest mountain is a freestanding volcano, not part of a range, and thousands of trekkers climb it each year without technical gear.
Places in Tanzania.Serengeti: Its Maasai-derived name means endless plains, and over a million wildebeest migrate through each year in the planet's largest land mammal movement.
Places in Tanzania.Zanzibar: This semi-autonomous island archipelago was a major spice and trading hub, and Stone Town is a World Heritage Site.
Places in Tanzania.Dar es Salaam: Its name means Haven of Peace in Arabic, and it is Tanzania's largest city, though not its official capital.
Places in Tanzania.Ngorongoro: A collapsed volcanic caldera about 20 kilometers wide, it shelters a dense population of wildlife, including endangered black rhinos.
Places in Tanzania.Dodoma: Tanzania's official capital since the 1970s, it sits inland, far less famous than Dar es Salaam, the larger coastal city.
Places in Tanzania.Arusha: The safari gateway city also hosted the Rwandan genocide tribunal, and Mount Meru rises just behind it.
Places in Tanzania.Lake Manyara: Famous for tree-climbing lions, this alkaline lake park is dotted with flamingos and sits below a steep rift wall.
Places in Tanzania.Mafia Island: Despite the name, it has nothing to do with gangsters; it is a diving paradise where whale sharks gather.
Places in Tanzania.Masai Mara: Kenya's famous reserve is the northern extension of the Serengeti ecosystem, so it lies across the border.
Places in Tanzania.Nairobi: Kenya's capital is unusual for having a national park of lions and giraffes within city limits.
Places in Tanzania.Mombasa: Kenya's main port city is on the Indian Ocean, home to the 16th-century Fort Jesus built by the Portuguese.
Places in Tanzania.Mount Kenya: Africa's second-highest mountain is, as its name hints, in Kenya, and straddles the equator with glaciers.
Places in Tanzania.Amboseli: A Kenyan park famed for elephants with Kilimanjaro in the backdrop, though the mountain itself lies in Tanzania.
Places in Tanzania.Lamu: This Kenyan island town is East Africa's oldest continuously inhabited Swahili settlement, with donkeys outnumbering cars.
Places in Tanzania.Kampala: The capital of Uganda is built on seven hills, much like Rome, and sits near Lake Victoria.
Places in Tanzania.Kigali: Rwanda's capital is known for being one of Africa's cleanest cities, with plastic bags banned since 2008.
Places in Tanzania.Lake Turkana: The world's largest permanent desert lake lies in northern Kenya and is nicknamed the Jade Sea for its color.
Places in Tanzania.Tsavo: Kenya's largest park, once made infamous by maneating lions that killed railway workers in 1898.
Places in Tanzania.Lalibela: This Ethiopian town is known for 11 churches carved from solid rock, a pilgrimage site of the Orthodox faith.
Places in Tanzania.Mogadishu: The capital of Somalia, a coastal city on the Indian Ocean far to the north of Tanzania.
Places in Tanzania.Luanda: Angola's capital sits on the Atlantic coast, on the opposite side of the continent from Tanzania.
Places in Tanzania.Mount Elgon: An extinct volcano on the Kenya-Uganda border, noted for caves where elephants mine salt from the walls.
Places in Tanzania.Addis Ababa: Ethiopia's capital, whose name means New Flower, sits at over 2,300 meters and hosts the African Union.

Things associated with Japan.Sushi: It began as a way to preserve fish in fermenting rice, and the rice was discarded until people started eating it.
Things associated with Japan.Kimono: Its name means thing to wear, and the way the left side crosses over the right is reversed only for the dead.
Things associated with Japan.Samurai: This warrior class lost its privileges in the 1870s, when Japan modernised and abolished the class system.
Things associated with Japan.Origami: Its name means folding paper, from ori and kami, and traditional models include the crane, said to bring luck with 1,000 folds.
Things associated with Japan.Bonsai: The art of growing miniature trees in pots, where some trees are centuries old.
Things associated with Japan.Shinkansen: The bullet train, opened in 1964, has no passenger deaths from crashes or derailments in its history.
Things associated with Japan.Karaoke: The word means empty orchestra, and it was invented in Japan in the 1970s, often credited to Daisuke Inoue.
Things associated with Japan.Haiku: A poem with 5, 7, and 5 syllables, and the master Basho made it famous in the 1600s.
Things associated with Japan.Sumo: Wrestlers throw salt into the ring to purify it before bouts, a ritual from Shinto.
Things associated with Japan.Manga: Japanese comics are read right to left, and are a huge share of the country's publishing industry.
Things associated with Japan.Anime: Japanese animation, with Studio Ghibli's Spirited Away winning an Oscar in 2003.
Things associated with Japan.Geisha: Trained artists of music, dance, and conversation, called geiko in Kyoto.
Things associated with Japan.Kimchi: Spicy fermented cabbage is the Korean national dish, and families traditionally make huge batches each autumn.
Things associated with Japan.K-pop: South Korea's polished pop machine, with idol groups trained for years, is a Korean export, not Japanese.
Things associated with Japan.Taekwondo: This Korean martial art, known for high kicks, became an Olympic sport in 2000, and it is not Japanese.
Things associated with Japan.Dim sum: Small shared dishes served with tea originated in Cantonese teahouses of southern China.
Things associated with Japan.Kung fu: A broad family of Chinese martial arts, famously practised at the Shaolin Temple, not a Japanese art.
Things associated with Japan.Pho: Vietnam's beefy noodle soup, which spread worldwide after 1975, so it isn't Japanese.
Things associated with Japan.Pad thai: The stir-fried noodle dish was promoted in the 1930s and 40s as part of building Thai national identity.
Things associated with Japan.Hanbok: Korea's traditional dress with a short jacket and wide skirt, not to be mistaken for the kimono.
Things associated with Japan.Qipao: A close-fitting Chinese dress with a high collar, popular in 1920s Shanghai, and not Japanese.
Things associated with Japan.Tuk-tuk: The three-wheeled motorised taxi is a Thai icon, named for the sound of its engine, not Japanese.
Things associated with Japan.Batik: This wax-resist dyeing technique is best known from Indonesia, where UNESCO honoured it in 2009.
Things associated with Japan.Yoga: India's ancient practice of postures, breath and meditation, not Japanese, though Zen has its own seated meditation.

Things you could extract DNA from.Banana: Bananas are a classic school experiment, as mashed fruit plus soap and salt lets DNA clump into visible strands. Most are clones, so they share the same DNA.
Things you could extract DNA from.Mushroom: Fungi have DNA like all life. Their genomes show mushrooms are more closely related to animals than to plants.
Things you could extract DNA from.Human hair root: The shaft is dead, but the root has living cells with DNA. That's why a pulled hair, not a cut one, helps in forensic tests.
Things you could extract DNA from.Bacteria: A single bacterium has a looping chromosome of about a few million DNA letters. Bacterial DNA was used to prove DNA carries heredity.
Things you could extract DNA from.Oak leaf: Leaves are full of cells with DNA. Plant genomes can be huge: some trees have more DNA than humans.
Things you could extract DNA from.Mosquito: Scientists sequence mosquito DNA to track disease and design gene drives. The 'Jurassic Park' idea of cloning from fossil blood is mostly fiction.
Things you could extract DNA from.Yeast: The same single-celled fungus that makes bread rise and beer ferment. Its genome, finished in 1996, was the first complete one for a complex cell.
Things you could extract DNA from.Coral: Coral are animals with DNA, and they host algae with their own DNA. Researchers read it to understand why reefs bleach.
Things you could extract DNA from.Seaweed: Algae have DNA like all living cells. Some kinds of seaweed are used as a source of food and gel, and as research subjects.
Things you could extract DNA from.Salmon: Fish carry DNA in every cell. Purified salmon sperm DNA is even a standard, low-cost reagent in many molecular biology labs.
Things you could extract DNA from.Moss: One of the oldest land plant groups, and its DNA can be extracted. Moss is a model organism for studying how plants moved onto land.
Things you could extract DNA from.Sponge: Sponges are simple animals with no organs but they do have DNA. Their genes reveal ancestors of all animals.
Things you could extract DNA from.Strawberry: Strawberry is a classic classroom DNA experiment. Its cells are octoploid, with eight copies of each chromosome, so it gives lots of DNA.
Things you could extract DNA from.Diamond: A trap: diamond is pure carbon, never alive, so it has no DNA. A diamond could never have heredity.
Things you could extract DNA from.Glass: A nonliving material made from melted sand. Glass has no cells, so it holds no DNA.
Things you could extract DNA from.Plastic: Made from petroleum chemicals, not cells. Nothing alive made it, so it contains no DNA.
Things you could extract DNA from.Table salt: Salt is a mineral, sodium chloride, which has never been alive. It's actually used in DNA extraction recipes, though, to help the DNA clump.
Things you could extract DNA from.Water: Pure water has no DNA. Tap or pond water might hold some from microbes or fish, and scientists sample it for 'environmental DNA'.
Things you could extract DNA from.Granite: A rock made of minerals, never alive. It contains no DNA of its own.
Things you could extract DNA from.Iron: A metal element, not a living thing, so no DNA. Your own blood needs iron, though, for hemoglobin.
Things you could extract DNA from.Sand: Tiny mineral grains, never alive, so no DNA. Beach sand may hold traces from microbes living in it.
Things you could extract DNA from.Steel: An alloy with no cells in it, so no DNA. Forensic experts can still find DNA on a blade, from whoever touched it.
Things you could extract DNA from.Gold: A metal, nonliving, so no DNA in it. Gold nanoparticles can be attached to DNA, though, in some lab tests.
Things you could extract DNA from.Red blood cell: A trap: mature human red blood cells lose their nucleus, so they contain no nuclear DNA at all. White blood cells provide the DNA in blood tests.

Films featuring time travel.Back to the Future: Marty McFly's DeLorean needs 88 miles per hour. Eric Stoltz was first cast as Marty and replaced by Michael J. Fox after about five weeks of filming.
Films featuring time travel.Looper: Rian Johnson's 2012 film, with Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Bruce Willis as younger and older versions of the same man, who is a hitman killing time-traveling targets.
Films featuring time travel.The Terminator: James Cameron's 1984 film sends a cyborg assassin back to 1984. It was made on a small budget and made Schwarzenegger a star.
Films featuring time travel.About Time: Richard Curtis's romantic comedy lets a man travel by clenching his fists in a dark closet. The film's lesson is more about living than about time.
Films featuring time travel.Tenet: Christopher Nolan's film features inverted entropy, so people move backward in time. He crashed a real Boeing 747 for a scene instead of using effects.
Films featuring time travel.Avengers: Endgame: The Avengers go back in time through the Quantum Realm to retrieve the Infinity Stones. The film became one of the highest-grossing movies ever.
Films featuring time travel.Midnight in Paris: Woody Allen's film sends Owen Wilson back to the 1920s every midnight, and it won him the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay.
Films featuring time travel.Kate & Leopold: A romantic comedy with Meg Ryan and Hugh Jackman, in which a duke from 1876 is pulled through a portal to modern-day New York.
Films featuring time travel.12 Monkeys: Terry Gilliam's 1995 film was inspired by La Jetee, a 1962 French short made almost entirely of still photographs.
Films featuring time travel.Somewhere in Time: A 1980 film with Christopher Reeve, who travels to the past by self-hypnosis, and it gained cult status over time.
Films featuring time travel.Meet the Robinsons: A 2007 Disney film in which a boy meets his future family, and it ends with the motto Keep moving forward.
Films featuring time travel.The Time Machine: Based on H.G. Wells's 1895 novel, it follows an inventor who travels to the far future. The 1960 film won an Oscar for special effects.
Films featuring time travel.Inception: This film is about shared dreams, not time travel. Time passes differently across dream layers, which makes it tempting, but nobody leaves the present.
Films featuring time travel.The Matrix: Humans are trapped in a simulation, so its world is fake, not a past. Its bullet time effect is more famous than any time travel.
Films featuring time travel.Gravity: Alfonso Cuaron's film is about astronauts stranded in orbit. It's a real-time survival story, not time travel.
Films featuring time travel.Titanic: Titanic is told via flashbacks as an old woman remembers. Memory is not time travel, so it doesn't fit.
Films featuring time travel.Up: Pixar's 2009 film has a house lifted by balloons, not a time machine. Its time-crossing is a montage of a long marriage.
Films featuring time travel.Jaws: A shark thriller with no time travel. Its release in 1975 gave rise to the summer blockbuster.
Films featuring time travel.Alien: A horror film set on a spaceship, which travels in space but not through time. Its crew sleeps in hypersleep for long voyages.
An alien who wants to go home, no time travel here. The film features Elliott's bike flying across the moon.
Films featuring time travel.Big: A boy wakes up in an adult body after a wish. It's a wish film, not time travel, so it doesn't fit.
Films featuring time travel.Freaky Friday: A mother and daughter swap bodies, not time periods. Time stays the same, so it doesn't fit.
Films featuring time travel.The Truman Show: Jim Carrey's Truman lives in a fake TV set, but time moves forward like normal. No time travel.
Films featuring time travel.Inside Out: This Pixar film is about emotions in a girl's head. Memories are important, but nobody travels in time.

Dance crazes.Macarena: Los del Rio's 1993 song spent 14 weeks at number one on the US Hot 100 in 1996, driven by its easy line dance.
Dance crazes.The Twist: Chubby Checker's 1960 hit is the only song to reach number one on the Billboard chart in two separate runs, in 1960 and 1962.
Dance crazes.Gangnam Style: PSY's 2012 video was the first on YouTube to pass a billion views, and its horse-riding dance spread worldwide.
Dance crazes.The Floss: Made famous by the Backpack Kid, swinging your hips and arms went global through Fortnite in 2018.
Dance crazes.Electric Slide: Created in 1976 by Ric Silver, set to Marcia Griffiths' Electric Boogie, it's a staple of weddings.
Dance crazes.Cha Cha Slide: DJ Casper made it in Chicago around 2000, reportedly for his niece who taught aerobics.
Dance crazes.YMCA: Village People's 1978 hit, with arms making the letters, was inspired by the real YMCA.
Dance crazes.The Hustle: Van McCoy's 1975 disco hit launched a line dance of the same name that dominated clubs.
Dance crazes.Harlem Shake: The 2013 meme was a short video clip, not the original Harlem Shake dance from the 1980s.
Dance crazes.Dab: A hip-hop gesture from Atlanta, popularised by Cam Newton and others around 2015.
Dance crazes.Chicken Dance: Swiss accordionist Werner Thomas wrote it in the 1950s; it's now an Oktoberfest staple.
Dance crazes.The Loco-Motion: Little Eva, Carole King's babysitter, sang this 1962 hit, which got to number one twice, first by her and then Grand Funk.
Dance crazes.Running Man: A 1980s hip-hop move that looks like jogging in place, popular long before its 2010s revival.
Dance crazes.Waltz: Once considered scandalous because dancers held each other, it's now a classic, not a craze.
Dance crazes.Tango: Born in Buenos Aires around the late 1800s, it's a cultural icon, not a passing fad.
Dance crazes.Ballet: Developed in French and Italian courts from the 1500s, ballet is a formal art, not a fad.
Dance crazes.Foxtrot: Named for vaudevillian Harry Fox in 1914, it's a ballroom standard, not a craze.
Dance crazes.Minuet: A stately 17th-century French court dance, long since a classical form rather than a fad.
Dance crazes.Polka: Czech in origin, 'polka' means 'half-step', and it swept Europe in the 1840s, but it's now a folk standard.
Dance crazes.Flamenco: Spain's flamenco is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage, not a short-lived craze.
Dance crazes.Hula: A Hawaiian dance telling stories with hands and hips, traditional rather than a fad.
Dance crazes.Quickstep: A fast ballroom dance, a standard in competitions, not a craze.
Dance crazes.Tap dance: Rhythmic footwork with metal taps; Gene Kelly and Fred Astaire made it famous, but it's a lasting genre.
Dance crazes.Rumba: Cuban in origin and sometimes called the dance of love, it's a ballroom standard, not a fad.

Animals that purr.Cat: A cat's purr hums at about 25 to 150 Hz, a range that may help bones and tissues heal.
Animals that purr.Cheetah: Cheetahs purr loudly, even while breathing in and out, but can't roar, unlike lions and tigers.
Animals that purr.Puma: Pumas can purr and scream, but can't roar, despite being large.
Animals that purr.Lynx: Lynxes purr like other small cats, though their cough-like calls are more famous.
Animals that purr.Bobcat: Bobcats purr too, along with growls and a cat-like scream.
Animals that purr.Ocelot: Ocelots purr, and their spotted coats were once prized by hunters.
Animals that purr.Serval: Servals purr and have huge ears to hear prey underground.
Animals that purr.Snow leopard: Despite being a big cat, it can't roar but it can purr and chuff.
Animals that purr.Guinea pig: Guinea pigs purr when content, and also wheek loudly when they see food.
Animals that purr.Dog: Dogs bark, growl and whine, but they don't purr; the closest is a soft, rumbling growl of pleasure.
Animals that purr.Horse: Horses nicker and whinny, not purr, and they can sleep standing up thanks to a locking joint in their legs.
Animals that purr.Cow: Cows moo, and studies suggest they have regional accents, with distinct herd calls.
Animals that purr.Snake: Snakes hiss, since they have no vocal cords, and feel vibrations through their jaws.
Animals that purr.Owl: Owls hoot, screech and hiss, and a barn owl's heart-shaped face channels sound like a dish.
Animals that purr.Duck: Ducks quack, and the old claim that a duck's quack doesn't echo is false.
Animals that purr.Frog: Frogs croak by inflating vocal sacs, not purring, and the loudest frog calls can be heard from a mile away.
Animals that purr.Elephant: Elephants rumble at infrasonic frequencies, low enough to travel kilometres, but that isn't a cat's purr.
Animals that purr.Shark: Sharks make almost no sound, so no purring from them, and their skeletons are made of cartilage.
Animals that purr.Penguin: Penguins bray and trumpet, and each bird recognises its mate's call in a noisy crowd.
Animals that purr.Goat: Goats bleat, and have rectangular pupils that give them a wide field of view.
Animals that purr.Parrot: Parrots mimic sounds, and some can copy human speech, but purring isn't one of the tricks.
Animals that purr.Sheep: Sheep bleat, and a lamb can recognise its mother's voice among hundreds.
Animals that purr.Pig: Pigs grunt and squeal, and they're smarter than many believe.
Animals that purr.Chicken: Chickens use over twenty distinct calls, including warnings for different predators, but no purr.

Soccer positions.Goalkeeper: The only player allowed to handle the ball in open play, and they wear a different colour shirt so referees can tell them apart.
Soccer positions.Striker: Forwards who lead the line are judged on goals, and the all-time international record belongs to Cristiano Ronaldo.
Soccer positions.Winger: Hugging the touchline, wingers stretch defences wide; the position's name comes from the wide, wing-like areas of the pitch.
Soccer positions.Centre-back: Usually paired in the heart of defence, they are often the tallest outfield players and win most of the aerial duels.
Soccer positions.Full-back: Once purely defenders, modern full-backs often run the length of the touchline, and some are now among the game's best creators.
Soccer positions.Sweeper: A free defender who roams behind the back line; Franz Beckenbauer redefined the role in the 1970s.
Soccer positions.Midfielder: The engine room, covering more ground than anyone else; top midfielders run about 11 to 13 km in a match.
Soccer positions.Wing-back: A hybrid of winger and full-back, essential in formations with three centre-backs and a wide-running flank.
Soccer positions.Playmaker: Less a fixed spot than a role: the creative midfielder, often in a number 10 shirt, who unlocks the defence with passes.
Soccer positions.Libero: Italian for free, it is the old name for the sweeper, a player who's free from marking duties and starts attacks from the back.
Soccer positions.Defender: A broad term for the back line; Italian teams of the 1960s made rock-solid defending an art form known as catenaccio.
Soccer positions.Quarterback: American football's passer; that sport's position, so it doesn't belong on a soccer pitch.
Soccer positions.Pitcher: Baseball's thrower; soccer has no mound, and nobody pitches in it.
Soccer positions.Shortstop: A baseball infielder between second and third base, with no equivalent in soccer.
Soccer positions.Point guard: A basketball position, the team's ball handler and play-caller, not a soccer role.
Soccer positions.Wicketkeeper: The cricketer who stands behind the stumps; unlike a goalkeeper, they play on a cricket field.
Soccer positions.Fly-half: A rugby union playmaker who wears number 10, a role in soccer's neighbouring code, not in soccer itself.
Soccer positions.Tight end: An American football hybrid of blocker and receiver, with no soccer counterpart.
Soccer positions.Linebacker: An American football defender who stops runs and covers passes; soccer does not have this position.
Soccer positions.Catcher: A baseball player who crouches behind home plate, wearing heavy protective gear.
Soccer positions.Setter: Volleyball's playmaker, who sets up teammates for attacking hits; soccer has no such role.
Soccer positions.Power forward: A basketball position known for strength near the basket; despite the word forward, it is not a soccer role.
Soccer positions.Small forward: A basketball wing, usually the most versatile scorer on court, and no relation to soccer's forwards.
Soccer positions.Running back: An American football ball carrier who takes handoffs; the only runners in soccer are the ones off the ball.

Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Anubis: The jackal-headed god of embalming; black, the color of fertile Nile silt and of rebirth, was his color.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Horus: Falcon-headed sky god whose eye, the Eye of Horus, became a symbol of protection and gave us a fraction system.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Thoth: The ibis- or baboon-headed god of writing and wisdom, said to have invented hieroglyphs and recorded the weighing of hearts.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Sobek: A crocodile-headed god, honored at Kom Ombo and Faiyum, where sacred crocodiles were once mummified.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Bastet: Originally a lioness, she turned into the cat goddess; killing a cat in ancient Egypt could be punishable by death.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Sekhmet: The lioness-headed goddess of war and healing; legend says Ra sent her to punish humankind and she nearly wiped them out.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Khnum: Ram-headed creator who shaped humans on a potter's wheel and was linked to the Nile's source at Elephantine.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Ra: The falcon-headed sun god, crowned with a sun disk, who traveled across the sky in a boat.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Set: His head is a mystery animal that scholars call the 'Set animal', with a curved snout and square-tipped ears.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Khepri: A scarab-headed god of the rising sun, who pushes the sun across the sky like a dung beetle rolls its ball.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Isis: A trap: she's shown as a woman, wearing a throne-shaped crown, though she is sometimes winged.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Osiris: A trap: the god of the dead is shown as a mummified man with a green or black face, with no animal head.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Ptah: Creator god of Memphis, shown as a man in a tight shroud, holding a staff; he has no animal head.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Nephthys: Sister of Isis, shown as a woman with a house-and-basket glyph on her head, not an animal.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Maat: Goddess of truth and balance, shown as a woman wearing an ostrich feather, which is weighed against hearts in the afterlife.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Aten: A sun disk with rays ending in hands, worshipped by Akhenaten, not a god with an animal head.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Nut: Sky goddess, shown as an arched woman covered in stars, and said to swallow the sun each evening.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Geb: Earth god, usually shown as a man lying beneath his sky wife Nut; earthquakes were said to be his laughter.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Shu: God of air, shown as a man holding up the sky; he separated the sky from earth, and has no animal head.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Minotaur: A trap: this bull-headed monster is Greek, from Crete, not Egyptian; Egypt's animal-headed gods are different.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Imhotep: A real architect and doctor, designer of the Step Pyramid, later deified; always shown as a man.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Cleopatra: A queen of the Greek Ptolemaic dynasty, not a god, and likely the first of her family to learn Egyptian.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Tutankhamun: A boy pharaoh of about 1330 BC, who is famous because his tomb was found nearly intact in 1922.
Egyptian gods usually shown with an anim.Nefertiti: Queen of Akhenaten, famous for her painted bust in Berlin, and shown as a woman, never as an animal-headed god.

Afterlife realms in mythology.Valhalla: Odin's hall for warriors slain in battle, who feast and fight daily until Ragnarok, when they will join the gods against the giants.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Elysium: Greek paradise for heroes and the virtuous, a land of gentle breezes and eternal spring. Later Romans reused the name, and Paris's Champs-Élysées echoes it.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Tartarus: A pit below even Hades where Zeus locked the Titans. Tantalus and Sisyphus were punished there, and Hesiod said an anvil would fall nine days to reach it.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Duat: The Egyptian underworld, crossed by the sun god's boat each night. There the dead heart was weighed against a feather, and a failed soul was eaten by Ammit.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Helheim: The realm of the goddess Hel, to which most Norse dead went, not just the cowardly. Its gate was guarded by the hound Garm, and Baldr was held there.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Folkvangr: Freyja's meadow where she receives half of those slain in battle, while Odin takes the rest to Valhalla. Her hall there is called Sessrúmnir.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Asphodel Meadows: Where ordinary Greek souls drifted, neither rewarded nor punished. Asphodel is a real pale flower, and a dull fate there is the point.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Xibalba: The Maya underworld, whose name means "place of fright". In the Popol Vuh, the Hero Twins beat its lords at a ball game and tricked their way to victory.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Mictlan: The Aztec land of the dead, reached after a four-year journey past nine levels. A dog was often buried with the deceased to guide them across the river.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Aaru: Egypt's Field of Reeds, an idyllic mirror of the Nile valley where the blessed dead farmed endlessly abundant wheat. Small servant figures did the work for them.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Yomi: The Japanese land of the dead. Izanagi fled it after seeing his decayed wife Izanami, and sealed the exit with a boulder.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Asgard: Home of the Norse gods, not the dead. Valhalla is a hall inside it, which is why Asgard fits the wider myth but not the afterlife category.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Midgard: The Norse world of humans, ringed by the sea serpent Jörmungandr. It is where the living dwell, so it is no afterlife. The word echoes in Tolkien's Middle-earth.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Olympus: Greece's highest mountain, about 2,900 metres, and the home of the twelve gods. A home for the living deities, not a place for the dead.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Atlantis: A lost island civilisation invented by Plato as a moral tale, then swallowed by the sea. It is an imaginary city, not an afterlife.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Camelot: King Arthur's legendary court, first named in 12th-century French romance. It was a seat of the living, never a place for the dead.
Afterlife realms in mythology.El Dorado: Originally a Muisca chief covered in gold dust, it grew into a legendary golden city that drew Spanish expeditions. Treasure, not afterlife.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Bifrost: The flaming rainbow bridge linking Midgard to Asgard, guarded by Heimdall. It is a road between worlds, not a realm of the dead.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Troy: The real city, probably in northwest Turkey, besieged in Homer's Iliad. A city of the living, though many died beneath its walls.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Jotunheim: The Norse land of the giants, a cold wild borderland. Thor made frequent trips there, but nobody went there when they died.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Shangri-La: A hidden paradise from James Hilton's 1933 novel Lost Horizon. Its inhabitants barely age, but they are living people, not the dead.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Ithaca: Odysseus's real island kingdom off western Greece, which he took ten years to reach after Troy. Home to the living and the goal of his journey.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Alfheim: Home of the light elves in Norse myth, given to Freyr as a teething gift. It is a realm of elves, not a place for the departed.
Afterlife realms in mythology.Vanaheim: The land of the Vanir gods, a fertility-minded tribe who once warred with the Aesir. It is a divine home, not an afterlife.

Cities of ancient Greece.Athens: Named for Athena, it was the home of Socrates and Plato. Its democracy let male citizens vote in an assembly, and juries were picked by lottery.
Cities of ancient Greece.Sparta: A militaristic city-state whose boys left home at seven to train as soldiers. Its women had unusual freedom and property rights for Greece.
Cities of ancient Greece.Corinth: A wealthy trading city on a narrow isthmus, where ships were dragged overland between two seas. It gave its name to the ornate Corinthian column.
Cities of ancient Greece.Thebes: The Greek Thebes was the legendary home of Oedipus and Antigone. Don't mix it up with Egyptian Thebes, now Luxor.
Cities of ancient Greece.Delphi: Home to the oracle of Apollo, where the priestess Pythia gave cryptic prophecies. The Greeks considered it the centre of the world.
Cities of ancient Greece.Olympia: The site of the ancient Olympic Games, held from 776 BC every four years in honour of Zeus. The modern Games began in 1896.
Cities of ancient Greece.Argos: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, in the Peloponnese. In legend, Heracles was a hero here, and it was a rival of Sparta.
Cities of ancient Greece.Mycenae: Bronze Age stronghold of King Agamemnon in Homer. Its entrance is the Lion Gate, and a gold mask found there was called his, though it is older.
Cities of ancient Greece.Megara: A Greek city between Athens and Corinth that sent out colonists, including to found Byzantium. Its pottery and a notorious blockade helped start the Peloponnesian War.
Cities of ancient Greece.Pylos: Home of the wise Nestor in the Iliad. Archaeologists found thousands of clay tablets in its palace, including Linear B records.
Cities of ancient Greece.Rome: Italian, not Greek. According to legend it was founded in 753 BC by Romulus, and it later conquered the Greek cities.
Cities of ancient Greece.Carthage: A Phoenician colony in what is now Tunisia, a Mediterranean rival to Rome. Hannibal marched from it to Italy.
Cities of ancient Greece.Babylon: A Mesopotamian city on the Euphrates, far to the east. The Greeks described it, as with the Hanging Gardens, but it was not Greek.
Cities of ancient Greece.Troy: Famous in Greek myth, but a real city in Anatolia, in modern Turkey. Greeks fought against it, not in it.
Cities of ancient Greece.Memphis: Egypt's ancient capital, south of modern Cairo, and not the Tennessee city. It was founded some 3,000 years before Greek power peaked.
Cities of ancient Greece.Persepolis: A ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire, burned by Alexander the Great in 330 BC. The Greek invaders destroyed it.
Cities of ancient Greece.Jerusalem: A city in the Levant, sacred to three religions. It was Hebrew, then Roman-ruled, but never a Greek polis.
Cities of ancient Greece.Pompeii: A Roman town in Italy, buried by Vesuvius in AD 79. It was Greek in some influence, but it was an Italian city.
Cities of ancient Greece.Nineveh: The Assyrian capital on the Tigris, in modern Iraq. It was destroyed in 612 BC, long before Greece's classical heyday.
Cities of ancient Greece.Ur: A Sumerian city in Iraq dating back about 6,000 years. It is far older and farther east than Greek cities.
Cities of ancient Greece.Tyre: A Phoenician port in Lebanon, famed for purple dye. Alexander the Great besieged it for seven months in 332 BC but it was not Greek.
Cities of ancient Greece.Petra: A Nabataean city in Jordan, carved in rose-red sandstone. It was a caravan hub, far from Greece.
Cities of ancient Greece.Damascus: A Syrian city, claimed to be one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities. Alexander's heirs held it, yet it was never a Greek polis.
Cities of ancient Greece.Luxor: The Egyptian city on the site of ancient Thebes, famed for Karnak and the Valley of the Kings. It is in Egypt, not Greece.

Medieval jobs.Blacksmith: Worked iron at the forge and made tools, horseshoes and weapons. The surname Smith is common in English because every village needed one.
Medieval jobs.Squire: A knight's apprentice, usually a teenager, who carried arms and cared for horses. Many squires fought in battle alongside their knights.
Medieval jobs.Jester: A court entertainer who could often say what nobles could not, since fool's licence protected jokes. Their cap and bells were part of the uniform.
Medieval jobs.Minstrel: A travelling singer and storyteller who carried news between towns. Many were paid by noble courts, others lived by tips on the road.
Medieval jobs.Falconer: Trained hawks and falcons for hunting. A bird's rank was strictly linked to its owner's: kings flew gyrfalcons, while a "knave" had a kestrel.
Medieval jobs.Cooper: Made barrels from wooden staves held by metal hoops, with no nails or glue. They were essential for storing beer, wine and fish.
Medieval jobs.Fletcher: Made arrows, often with goose feathers. The French word flèche means arrow, and Fletcher became a common surname, as did Bowyer for bowmakers.
Medieval jobs.Tanner: Turned animal hides into leather, using a smelly process involving lime and dung or urine. Tanneries were therefore often built at the edge of town.
Medieval jobs.Scribe: Copied manuscripts by hand. Monks working in a scriptorium might spend months or years on a single Bible.
Medieval jobs.Herald: Carried messages for lords and recognised knights by their coats of arms. The craft of heraldry developed as visors hid faces.
Medieval jobs.Monk: Lived in a community under vows, often copying books, tending herbs and sometimes brewing. A monastery was also school, hospital and inn.
Medieval jobs.Chandler: Made candles from tallow (animal fat) or beeswax. Tallow stank, and only the rich could afford beeswax.
Medieval jobs.Astronaut: Only in 1961 did the first human, Yuri Gagarin, reach space. The job is modern, and no medieval person could have held it.
Medieval jobs.Barista: A coffee-bar worker, from Italian. Coffee was unknown in Europe until after the Middle Ages.
Medieval jobs.Software engineer: A job that needs computers, invented in the 20th century. The word software dates from 1958.
Medieval jobs.Electrician: Needs electric power networks, which started in the 1880s. A medieval job needed fire and iron.
Medieval jobs.Pilot: A pilot flying an aircraft appeared after the Wright brothers' flight in 1903. Medieval "pilots" only steered ships into harbour.
Medieval jobs.DJ: The disc jockey needs recorded music and radio. The first radio DJ broadcast came in the early 1900s.
Medieval jobs.Influencer: A social media job from the 2010s. In the Middle Ages, fame spread by minstrels and heralds.
Medieval jobs.Photographer: The first lasting photos date from the 1820s. The word "photography" was coined in 1839.
Medieval jobs.Taxi driver: Taxi service needs motor vehicles, which emerged in the late 1800s. Hackney horse carriages came earlier, in the 1600s.
Medieval jobs.Radio host: Needs broadcast radio, which began in the 1920s. Medieval news came by town crier.
Medieval jobs.Stockbroker: Share trading began in the 1600s with the Dutch East India Company. It came after the Middle Ages.
Medieval jobs.Flight attendant: The first airline cabin crew, in 1930, were nurses on United Airlines. A medieval world had no commercial flights.

Things a seagull would steal.French fries: Studies of urban gulls show they often go for food that humans have just handled, and chips are a favorite thanks to their salty, easy-to-grab form.
Things a seagull would steal.Potato chips: Seagulls have been filmed snatching chips mid-bite, and research in Britain showed gulls are more likely to go after food that people are looking away from.
Things a seagull would steal.Sandwich: A gull will swoop on a sandwich in a split second, and the bird's strong, hooked bill makes grabbing the lot a simple matter.
Things a seagull would steal.Ice cream cone: Seaside gulls have a famous record for stealing cones straight from hands, and the cold sweet treat is one of their favorites.
Things a seagull would steal.Hot dog: Gulls are opportunistic omnivores that eat almost anything, so a hot dog at a ballpark or pier doesn't last long if you look away.
Things a seagull would steal.Donut: A donut is easy to carry off whole, and gulls will grab sugary snacks as readily as any other human food.
Things a seagull would steal.Pizza slice: Gulls in cities such as Venice and Boston have been seen snatching pizza slices, adapting well to human leftovers.
Things a seagull would steal.Pretzel: A pretzel's knotted shape fits neatly in a beak, and gulls will take them from beachgoers and boardwalks.
Things a seagull would steal.Popcorn: Popcorn is light and easy to scatter, and gulls will happily gobble it up from the ground, which is why feeding them is discouraged.
Things a seagull would steal.Bread roll: Bread is a gull's classic handout, though it is poor nutrition for them, and many seaside towns ask people not to feed them.
Things a seagull would steal.Fish and chips: A seaside tradition in Britain, and the gulls there are so notorious that some towns have hired hawks to scare them off from takeaway meals.
Things a seagull would steal.Beach umbrella: No bird could lift a beach umbrella, though gulls do like perching on the poles, and they will happily raid the bags beneath one.
Things a seagull would steal.Lifeguard tower: A tower can't be carried off, and gulls simply perch on its roof; the beach food it overlooks is what they are really after.
Things a seagull would steal.Surfboard: A surfboard is far too big for a gull to carry off, and gulls would rather perch on one than steal it, since there is no food on it.
Things a seagull would steal.Sandcastle: Gulls can't walk off with a sandcastle, but they may poke through it, since crabs and tiny sea creatures sometimes hide in beach sand.
Things a seagull would steal.Deck chair: A deck chair is too bulky and inedible; the gull's real target is the snack on the lap of the person sitting in it.
Things a seagull would steal.Kayak: A kayak weighs more than a gull's whole flock, and it has no food, so gulls leave it alone, except to perch on it.
Things a seagull would steal.Pier: Piers are favorite gull lookouts, where birds sit on the rails and watch for fishermen's bait or a dropped chip.
Things a seagull would steal.Lighthouse: Lighthouses are perches and nesting sites for seabirds, but the building itself is far too solid to steal.
Things a seagull would steal.Sailboat: Gulls love perching on a sailboat's mast, but a whole boat is far beyond what any bird could carry off.
Things a seagull would steal.Volleyball net: A net is of no interest to a gull, though birds can get tangled in loose netting, which is a hazard to them.
Things a seagull would steal.Jet ski: A jet ski weighs hundreds of kilograms and is not edible, so it is safe from even the boldest gull.
Things a seagull would steal.Bus: A bus is no gull's prey, but gulls do crowd bus stops and parking lots near the coast, watching for dropped food.
Things a seagull would steal.Picnic table: The table isn't what gets stolen, but a gull will happily wait on one for a careless diner to leave their food behind.

Things in a chef's kitchen.Whisk: A whisk adds air to cream and eggs, and the wire loops are what do the work.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Ladle: A ladle serves soups and stews, and its deep bowl is perfect for portioning.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Colander: A colander drains pasta, and the name comes from the Latin word colare, meaning to strain.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Mandoline: A mandoline slices vegetables to uniform thinness, and it's famously a source of kitchen injuries.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Rolling pin: A rolling pin flattens dough, and the tapered French pin has no handles at all.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Cleaver: A cleaver cuts through bone, and its wide blade also doubles for crushing garlic in Chinese cooking.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Saucepan: A saucepan has tall sides for sauces and liquids, and its name comes from the sauce it holds.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Tongs: Tongs let cooks turn hot food without burning their hands, and most chefs say they're their favorite tool.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Spatula: A spatula flips pancakes and eggs, and silicone ones can withstand high heat.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Peeler: A peeler removes skin in a thin layer, and the swivel-blade peeler is a Swiss invention from the 1940s.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Grater: A grater shreds cheese and vegetables, and the microplane version began as a woodworking rasp.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Mortar and pestle: A mortar and pestle is among the oldest kitchen tools, used for thousands of years to grind spices.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Wok: A wok's rounded bottom spreads heat for stir-frying, which was developed in China over 2,000 years ago.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Chisel: A chisel belongs to the woodworker's bench, and it's used to carve out joints.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Hacksaw: A hacksaw cuts metal, with a fine-toothed blade held in a frame.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Stethoscope: A stethoscope is a doctor's listening tool, which is why a chef wouldn't wear one.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Trowel: A trowel is a gardener's or mason's hand tool, for digging and spreading mortar.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Wrench: A wrench turns nuts and bolts, a toolbox item, not a kitchen item.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Pitchfork: A pitchfork is a farm tool for lifting hay, and the pitchfork of folklore is in the devil's hand.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Easel: An easel holds an artist's canvas, so it belongs in a studio.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Anvil: An anvil belongs to a blacksmith, and it can weigh well over a hundred pounds.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Sextant: A sextant measures the angle between a star and the horizon, so sailors can find their latitude.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Plunger: A plunger unblocks drains and is not for the kitchen, though it's often used in the sink.
Things in a chef's kitchen.Gavel: A gavel is a judge's or auctioneer's mallet, symbolizing the authority of the court.

Jobs done mostly outdoors.Lumberjack: Working outdoors in forests, in all weathers. The classic red plaid flannel actually became popular for being warm even when damp.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Farmer: Farmers spend their days in fields. Fewer than 2 percent of Americans farm today, compared with about half in the 1870s.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Lifeguard: Posted on beaches and pools, lifeguards scan for drowning, which is often quiet. Real drowning rarely looks like splashing and shouting.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Park ranger: Rangers patrol trails, campsites and wildlife areas, so they're often outside. The US National Park Service began in 1916.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Roofer: Working on rooftops in sun and wind, roofers face hot surfaces that can exceed 150 degrees Fahrenheit on summer days.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Gardener: Gardening outdoors is linked with lower stress. Soil bacteria like Mycobacterium vaccae may even affect mood.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Fisherman: Commercial fishing consistently ranks among the most dangerous jobs, due to weather, heavy gear and remote seas.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Landscaper: They design and tend outdoor spaces. A modern landscape architect profession began with Frederick Law Olmsted, designer of Central Park.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Shepherd: Shepherds have tended flocks outdoors for millennia. Herding dogs like border collies still do much of the actual work.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Surveyor: They measure land with tools such as theodolites and GPS. George Washington worked as a surveyor in his teens.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Golf caddie: A caddie carries the bag and offers advice on a course. The word is thought to come from French 'cadet', a younger son.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Mail carrier: Carriers walk or drive routes in all weather, and many log several miles on foot each day.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Accountant: Mostly an office job. Even the term 'bookkeeping' is ancient, with double-entry methods dating to medieval Italy.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Dentist: Dentists work inside clinics. Dentists in ancient times drilled teeth with bow-driven tools thousands of years ago.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Librarian: Librarians work indoors among books, though they now manage data and online resources just as much.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Barista: An Italian word meaning 'bartender', barista is indoors work, behind an espresso machine.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Pharmacist: They dispense medication from counters indoors. Pharmacies were once called apothecaries.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Programmer: Mostly desk-bound. Ada Lovelace's notes in the 1840s are often called the first computer program.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Bank teller: An indoors role, though bank tellers face fewer customers each year as online banking spreads.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Hairdresser: Work happens in salons. Chemically straightened or permed styles became mainstream only in the 20th century.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Receptionist: A front-desk role indoors. A receptionist is often the first person visitors meet, which shapes impressions greatly.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Data analyst: Analysts spend their days with spreadsheets and dashboards. It's the opposite of a field job.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Radiologist: Doctors who read X-rays and scans inside hospitals, often in dark rooms for better screen contrast.
Jobs done mostly outdoors.Baker: Bakers work in hot indoor kitchens, often starting well before dawn so bread is fresh by morning.

Common job perks.Health insurance: In the US, most working-age people get health insurance via an employer, a link that began during World War II wage controls.
Common job perks.Paid vacation: The US is one of the few rich countries with no federal law guaranteeing paid vacation, unlike most of Europe.
Common job perks.Company car: In some countries, including Germany and the UK, a company car is a standard status symbol and a taxable benefit.
Common job perks.Bonus: Bonuses are extra pay on top of salary, and in some industries they make up a major share of the annual income.
Common job perks.Stock options: Stock options give the right to buy shares at a fixed price, and they made many early tech employees rich.
Common job perks.Gym membership: A free gym is meant to keep staff healthy, and some employers claim it cuts sick days and health costs.
Common job perks.Free lunch: Google famously offers free meals, and it's one of the best-known perks in the tech world.
Common job perks.Pension: A pension pays a retirement income, and the first state pensions began in Germany in the 1880s.
Common job perks.Remote work: Remote work surged in 2020 and many workers now count it as a major benefit equal to extra pay.
Common job perks.Parental leave: Some countries, like Sweden, give parents over a year of paid shared leave, and some of it is reserved for each parent.
Common job perks.Sick days: Paid sick leave is a legal right in much of the world, but not federally in the US.
Common job perks.Pay cut: A pay cut reduces what you earn, so it's the opposite of a perk.
Common job perks.Unpaid overtime: Working off the clock may be illegal in many places, and it is definitely not a perk.
Common job perks.Layoffs: Layoffs are job cuts, so they are the opposite of a benefit.
Common job perks.Demotion: A demotion lowers your rank, which is a setback, not a perk.
Common job perks.Micromanagement: Being checked on constantly saps morale, and surveys regularly cite it as a top reason people quit.
Common job perks.Long commute: A long commute eats into your day, and studies link it with lower happiness, so it's a drawback.
Common job perks.Pay freeze: A freeze keeps pay unchanged, and with inflation it is effectively a cut.
Common job perks.Mandatory weekends: Required weekend work usually costs time off, so it's no perk, unless it comes with extra pay.
Common job perks.Salary deduction: A deduction takes money out of your pay, so no one would count it as a benefit.
Common job perks.Probation: Probation is a trial period when you can be let go easily, so it's a risk, not a perk.
Common job perks.Written warning: A written warning is a formal notice of poor conduct that can lead to dismissal, and it is no benefit.
Common job perks.Unpaid internship: Unpaid internships are controversial and sometimes illegal, and critics say they favor those who can afford to work for free.
Common job perks.Wage theft: Wage theft means not paying workers what they're owed, and it is illegal and costs workers billions of dollars a year.

Things a cowboy uses.Lasso: The word comes from the Spanish lazo, and the rope is traditionally braided from rawhide, which makes it strong and stiff.
Things a cowboy uses.Saddle: The classic Western saddle has a horn used to anchor a roped steer, and its design came from Spanish vaqueros.
Things a cowboy uses.Spurs: Spurs are worn on the heels to guide the horse, and the small jingling rowels give cowboy boots their famous sound.
Things a cowboy uses.Stetson: John B. Stetson made his wide-brimmed hat in 1865, and its tall crown could even carry water for a thirsty horse.
Things a cowboy uses.Chaps: Chaps are leather leg coverings that protect against brush and thorns, and the name comes from the Spanish chaparreras.
Things a cowboy uses.Bandana: A cowboy pulled a bandana up over his nose to block trail dust, and it also served as a sweat rag and a bandage.
Things a cowboy uses.Bridle: A bridle holds the bit and reins, and it lets the rider steer the horse by pressure on the mouth and neck.
Things a cowboy uses.Cowboy boots: The tall shaft and slanted heel were designed to stay in the stirrup and slide out easily if the rider fell.
Things a cowboy uses.Branding iron: Ranchers branded cattle with a registered mark, and cattle brands are still legally recorded in many states today.
Things a cowboy uses.Bedroll: A bedroll was the cowboy's portable bed, rolled up in a canvas sheet, and it was often the only comfort on a long trail drive.
Things a cowboy uses.Horse: Cowboys often owned several horses, since a "string" of mounts let each one rest, and a good cow horse could read a cow's moves.
Things a cowboy uses.Canteen: A canteen carried drinking water across the dry plains, and sometimes the cowboy's life depended on the little in it.
Things a cowboy uses.Surfboard: A surfboard is for waves, not prairies, though the American West also has a long and unrelated surfing history in California.
Things a cowboy uses.Briefcase: A briefcase is for office work, and the only case cowboys carried was maybe a saddlebag.
Things a cowboy uses.Snorkel: A snorkel is for swimming, and cowboys had far less call for water gear.
Things a cowboy uses.Tiara: Tiaras are royal head wear, and a cowboy's headgear is a big hat.
Things a cowboy uses.Kimono: A kimono is traditional Japanese dress and has no place on a cattle drive.
Things a cowboy uses.Monocle: A monocle is a single eyeglass lens, popular with dandies, and rarely seen in the Wild West.
Things a cowboy uses.Scuba tank: A scuba tank is for diving, and the Old West had plenty of dust but little deep water.
Things a cowboy uses.Skis: Skis are for snow, and while cowboys faced blizzards, they worked on horseback.
Things a cowboy uses.Top hat: The top hat is for formal city wear, so a cowboy's hat is the wide-brim Stetson.
Things a cowboy uses.Bowling ball: Bowling balls are heavy, and a cowboy would not carry one, though a saloon might have had a lane.
Things a cowboy uses.Umbrella: Cowboys used a slicker, a long oilskin coat, against rain, since an umbrella and a horse are an awkward combination.
Things a cowboy uses.Pogo stick: The pogo stick was invented in the early 1900s, and a cowboy would rather ride a horse than bounce.

Workplace safety gear.Hard hat: Hard hats became standard on U.S. construction sites in the 1930s, with the first ones at the Hoover Dam, where workers coated cloth hats with tar.
Workplace safety gear.Safety goggles: Goggles seal around the eyes to block dust and splashes, unlike ordinary glasses, which let particles enter from the side.
Workplace safety gear.Earplugs: Earplugs date back to Homer's Odyssey, where Odysseus uses beeswax to plug his crew's ears, and modern foam ones cut noise by about 30 decibels.
Workplace safety gear.Steel-toe boots: Steel-toe boots are rated to withstand a heavy impact and compression, and toe caps today are often composite materials too.
Workplace safety gear.Hi-vis vest: Hi-vis colors are fluorescent yellow-green, which the human eye detects well, plus reflective stripes that bounce back headlights at night.
Workplace safety gear.Respirator: A respirator filters out dust and fumes, and the rating N95 means it blocks at least 95 percent of tiny airborne particles.
Workplace safety gear.Work gloves: Cut-resistant work gloves woven with fibers such as Kevlar can stop a blade that would slice a leather glove.
Workplace safety gear.Face shield: A face shield guards against flying debris and splashes, but it doesn't protect from fine dust so it is worn together with goggles.
Workplace safety gear.Safety harness: A harness spreads the force of a fall across the thighs and chest, and falls from height are a top cause of construction deaths.
Workplace safety gear.Ear defenders: Ear defenders are earmuffs for protecting against loud noise, and long exposure above 85 decibels can damage hearing over time.
Workplace safety gear.Flip-flops: Flip-flops leave toes bare, so they're banned from most worksites, while the Japanese zori sandals inspired them.
Workplace safety gear.Necktie: A tie can get caught in machinery, and workers near moving parts are often told to remove them. The tie dates to Croatian soldiers' cravats.
Workplace safety gear.Necklace: A dangling necklace can snag on machinery, which is why jewelry is usually prohibited around moving parts.
Workplace safety gear.Sandals: Open toes risk crushed feet on a worksite, and sandals are among the oldest footwear, found in 10,000-year-old finds.
Workplace safety gear.Bow tie: A bow tie is formal wear, and it can't snag as easily as a necktie, but it's not safety gear.
Workplace safety gear.Cufflinks: Cufflinks fasten a dress shirt's cuff and are decoration, not protection.
Workplace safety gear.Bathrobe: A bathrobe is cozy at home, and it's no use on a work site, where loose fabric is a hazard.
Workplace safety gear.Slippers: Slippers are for indoors, and they offer little grip or protection against anything heavy.
Workplace safety gear.Tiara: A tiara is a jeweled head ornament for royalty, and it's no substitute for a hard hat.
Workplace safety gear.Toupee: A toupee is a hairpiece, and the word is French for a tuft of hair, and it doesn't protect anyone's head.
Workplace safety gear.Feather boa: A feather boa is a flashy accessory, and would be a hazard around machinery.
Workplace safety gear.Silk scarf: A scarf can catch in a machine, and scarf-related accidents famously ended the life of dancer Isadora Duncan in 1927.
Workplace safety gear.High heels: High heels were invented for horse riding, to hold the foot in the stirrup, and were worn by Persian cavalry.
Workplace safety gear.Mittens: Mittens keep fingers warm, but offer poor dexterity and little protection from cuts, so aren't work gloves.

Image file extensions..jpg: The JPEG format throws away detail you're unlikely to notice, and the three-letter extension comes from old DOS limits on name length.
Image file extensions..png: Created in the mid-1990s as a free replacement for GIF, PNG supports transparency and compresses without losing any quality.
Image file extensions..gif: Its creator, Steve Wilhite, said it was pronounced with a soft g, like the peanut butter, a debate that's never settled; it supports short looping animations.
Image file extensions..bmp: Bitmap files store every pixel with little or no compression, so they're often huge compared with a JPEG of the same image.
Image file extensions..tiff: TIFF is popular with photographers, scanners and print workflows because it keeps full quality, and it can hold multiple pages.
Image file extensions..webp: Google released WebP in 2010 to make web images smaller than JPEG and PNG at similar quality.
Image file extensions..svg: Scalable Vector Graphics describe shapes with math, not pixels, so they stay sharp at any size and can be edited as text.
Image file extensions..heic: This is the format iPhones have used by default since 2017, storing photos at about half the size of a JPEG.
Image file extensions..jpeg: The same format as .jpg: the shorter version exists only because early Windows limited extensions to three letters.
Image file extensions..ico: The icon format holds several sizes of one image in a single file, which is how a favicon appears in browser tabs.
Image file extensions..mp3: An audio format, made famous by shrinking songs to about a tenth of the CD size by dropping sounds you can barely hear.
Image file extensions..mp4: A video container, and one of the most common formats on the web, used by phones and streaming services.
Image file extensions..docx: A Word document, which is secretly a zipped bundle of XML files, as you can see by renaming it .zip.
Image file extensions..pdf: Created by Adobe in 1993 to look identical on any device; it can hold images but is a document format.
Image file extensions..zip: An archive, introduced by Phil Katz in 1989; it holds other files, so a zip may contain images but isn't one.
Image file extensions..exe: A Windows program, short for executable, and opening a surprise one from an email is a classic way to catch malware.
Image file extensions..wav: An uncompressed audio format from Microsoft and IBM, so it's perfectly accurate but takes up lots of space.
Image file extensions..txt: Plain text, so it has no formatting at all, which is why it will open on almost any device ever made.
Image file extensions..html: The file type of web pages; it describes text and links and can reference images, but it isn't one.
Image file extensions..csv: Comma-separated values store spreadsheet-style data as plain text, and are some of the simplest formats around.
Image file extensions..mov: Apple's QuickTime video container, introduced in 1991, and it's a movie rather than a picture.
Image file extensions..xls: The older Excel spreadsheet format, replaced by .xlsx in 2007.
Image file extensions..avi: A Microsoft video format from 1992, which is among the oldest around and still turns up.
Image file extensions..ppt: The older PowerPoint format, replaced by .pptx in 2007, and it's a slide deck, not an image.

Characters in Romeo and Juliet.Romeo: He pines for Rosaline until he sees Juliet at a party, falling in love so quickly that Friar Laurence is alarmed.
Characters in Romeo and Juliet.Juliet: She is not yet 14 in the play, and the famous balcony scene is never called a balcony in Shakespeare's text.
Characters in Romeo and Juliet.Mercutio: Romeo's witty friend curses 'A plague o' both your houses' as he dies, and his death turns the play toward tragedy.
Characters in Romeo and Juliet.Tybalt: Mercutio calls him the 'Prince of Cats', a nod to Tibert the cat in the old fable of Reynard the Fox.
Characters in Romeo and Juliet.Benvolio: Romeo's cousin, whose name means 'good will', tries to keep the peace and later recounts the tragic events.
Characters in Romeo and Juliet.Friar Laurence: The friar secretly marries the lovers and gives Juliet the sleeping potion, a plan that goes terribly wrong.
Characters in Romeo and Juliet.Paris: The nobleman engaged to marry Juliet is killed by Romeo at her tomb.
